questions.title: What practical benefit does exponential gating provide over standard sigmoid gating in sLSTM?
questions.question_body: In the sLSTM update equations, the input gate is defined as $i_t = 	ext{exp}(	ilde{i}_t)$ while traditionally it would be $i_t = 	ext{sigmoid}(	ilde{i}_t)$. The paper claims that exponential gating allows *revise storage decisions* and explains this with the Nearest Neighbor Search task. Could someone elaborate on how an exponential gate changes the dynamics of the cell state compared to a sigmoid gate? What happens to gradient flow and vanishing/exploding gradients when using $	ext{exp}$ instead of $	ext{sigmoid}$? Also, why is a separate stabilizer state $m_t$ needed, and how does it prevent overflow without affecting back‑propagated gradients?

questions.title: How does the new normalizer state $n_t$ in sLSTM enable memory mixing across heads?
questions.question_body: Equation (5) introduces a normalizer state $n_t$ that accumulates $i_t$ over time. The paper mentions that it "keeps record of the strength of the gates" and enables *memory mixing* when multiple heads are used. I am not sure how $n_t$ is used during mixing. Does it act only in $	ilde{h}_t = c_t / n_t$ or is it also involved in cross‑head interactions? If we have multiple heads with independent memory mixing, how is $n_t$ computed for each head, and does it influence inter‑head gating or just within‑head cell updates?

questions.question_body:
The paper states that scalar memory cells limit storage capacity and explains this via a Rare Token Prediction experiment on Wikitext‑103. While I see that a scalar $c_t$ needs to compress all information from previous steps into one number, I'm unclear why a matrix $	extbf{C}_t
e 	extbf{c}_t$ solves the problem. How exactly does the covariance update rule $	extbf{C}_t = 	extbf{C}_{t-1} + 	extbf{v}_t 	extbf{k}_t^	op$ allow a key/value pair to be stored independently? Does this change require additional parameters or extra hidden states? And why can we still retrieve with $	ilde{	extbf{h}}_t = 	extbf{C}_t	extbf{q}_t /  igl|	extbf{n}_t^	op	extbf{q}_t igr|$?

questions.title: In what way does exponential gating interact with the stabilizer state during training?
questions.question_body: Equation (6) defines $m_t =  iglfloor  igl(\\log(f_t)+m_{t-1}\bigr),\quad \log(i_t) igr)$ and then stabilizes gates as $i'_t=	extexp(	ilde{i}_t-m_t)$. However, it is not obvious how this construction preserves gradients. Could someone walk through a simple example (say one time step) showing that replacing $i_t$ by $i'_t$ and $f_t$ by $f'_t$ leaves output unchanged but also preserves exact gradients? I suspect something like a log‑softmax trick is used, but I would like to see the derivation.

questions.title: How can mLSTM be parallelised across layers despite having recurrent updates?
questions.question_body: $ m C_t=f_t m C_{t-1}+i_t m v_t m k_t^	op$ looks like a conventional recurrence because $ m C_{t-1}$ depends on previous time steps. The paper says mLSTM can be reformulated in a fully parallel version but provides no details. What are the mathematical steps to rewrite this as a scan-like or cumulative sum operation over the entire sequence? Does this involve pre‑computing cumulative products of forget gates or accumulative sums of outer products? Also, technically, what changes if we use softmax instead of exponential gates for $f_t$, or if we remove the stabilizer?

questions.title: What is the role of the output gate in mLSTM’s retrieval step?
questions.question_body: $	ilde{ m h}_t = ( m C_t  m q_t) /  igl| m n^	op  m q igr|$ gives us an unscaled retrieved vector from memory. The output gate then scales that vector elementwise: $ m h_t =  m o_t  oldsymbol{	ilde h}_t$. Why do we need an elementwise scaling after retrieval? Wouldn't setting $ m o_t= oldsymbol 1$ suffice for learning? What effect does an adaptive output gate have on alignment between stored keys and retrieved vectors?

questions.title: "Residual block with pre up‑projection" vs "post up‑projection": why choose different architectures for mLSTM vs sLSTM?
questions.question_body: Section 4.1 mentions using a post up‑projection block for sLSTM and a pre up‑projection block for mLSTM based on 'memory capacity becomes larger in high dimensional space.' Can someone clarify why memory capacity motivations lead to different block designs? Specifically, how does pre‑ vs post‑ projection affect the representation space for learning key/value embeddings versus cell updates? Are there empirical ablation results supporting this design choice?

questions.title: "Exponential gating" versus “mixing via ReLU or tanh” – could we replace exp with other nonlinearities?
questions.question_body: "Exponential gating" seems unique to xLSTM but other recent models use gated ReLU/LU activation functions (e.g., GLU). How would replacing $	extexp(	ilde{i})$ by say $	extit{relu}(	ilde{i})$ or even a learned temperature scale affect performance? Are there theoretical reasons why only exponentials are suitable when combining with covariance update rules?

questions.title: "Memory mixing” across heads – is it equivalent to multi‑head attention?
questions.question_body: The paper introduces 'memory mixing within each head but not across heads' as new way of memory mixing enabled by exponential gates. Is this analogous to multi-head self‑attention where each head attends independently? If so, can we view sLSTM’s memory mixing as performing self‑attention over past cell states, or is it fundamentally different because of recurrent dependencies?

questions.title: "Scaling behavior” figure shows xLSTM outperforming existing methods – could you explain what parameters were tuned for xLSTM and Transformer baselines?
questions.question_body: Several figures compare perplexity versus model size (Figure 8 & 9). However, I am unsure what hyperparameters were used for xLSTM vs Transformers: learning rates, weight decay, dropout rates etc. Were they matched exactly per layer or was xLSTM allowed more tuning? Could someone detail any differences that may influence fairness?

questions.title: "Residual stacking architecture” – how many layers/heads in xLSTM blocks correspond to 48 residual blocks?
questions.question_body: $x_	ext{text}{block}[a:b]$ notation seems confusing: If xLSTM[7:1] has 48 total blocks, does that mean 42 mLSTM-based blocks (7 heads?) and 6 sLSTM based blocks? How exactly are layers and heads counted in practice when building an architecture like 48 residual blocks? Also what dimension do you use for hidden states inside an individual block?

questions.title: "Zero‑mean key/value assumption” – how critical is centering before covariance update?

"The covariance update rule assumes zero mean keys/values" – what happens if we don't enforce this via layer norms? Would nonzero means bias the matrix memory leading to interference between different key/value pairs? Has anyone tried removing mean subtraction; if so does performance drop significantly?
